T
3
4
5 Abstract. The concept of degrowth has refuelled the criticism of unchecked econoPmic growth.
I
6 The purpose of this paper is to identify the central themes of the 21st century growth critique.
R
7 Qualitative content analysis is conducted for three contemporary classics of the expanding
C
8 degrowth literature: Peter Victor's Managing without growth: Slower by design, not disaster,
S
9 Serge Latouche's Farewell to Growth and Tim Jackson's Prosperity without growth: Economics
U
10 for a finite planet. The analysis reveals three central themes, which provide different
N
11 perspectives on growth: 1) Growth as a phenomenon, focusing on the forms and impacts of
A
12 growth and degrowth; 2) Growth as an institution, investigating institutions that either support
M
13 or depend on growth; 3) Growth as an ideology, perceiving economic growth as an
14 overwhelming and hegemonic political goal above other goals and the need for emancipation.
D
15 The themes complement each other. Together they provide a new framework for
E
16 understanding the diverse aspects of growth and degrowth. The analysis shows that the
T
17 growth critique is essentially a critique of growth societies, not only a critique of GDP growth
P
18 and that the growth critics are more elaborate in describing what they oppose than what they
E
19 support. An inner tension within growth critique regarding attitudes to agrowth and degrowth
C
20 is also revealed.
C
A
21 Keywords: economic growth, degrowth, qualitative content analysis
22 Highlights:
23 1. A qualitative content analysis was conducted on three books representing the 21st century
24 growth critique.

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
2
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 2. The analysis revealed three themes: economic growth as a phenomenon, an institution and
2 an ideology.
T
3 3. The first theme focuses on the forms and impacts of growth and degrowth.
P
4 4. The second theme emphasises the institutional structures that either support or are
I
R
5 dependent on growth.
C
6 5. The third theme views growth as a hegemonic political goal set above other goals.
S
7 1 Introduction U
8
N
9 The purpose of this paper is to identify and analyse the central themes of the contemporary
A
10 growth critique. Earlier debates on the volume of material production and consumption in the
M
11 economy are well-established. Malthus started the discussion about the discrepancy between
12 the growth rates of population and food pr oduction as early as two hundred years ago
D
13 (Malthus 1976). Economic growth became the main goal of public policies especially in the
E
14 USA in the decades after World War II (Collins 2002). As a reaction, the divergence of
T
15 economic growth and well-being was discussed elaborately. Galbraith (1958) considered the
P
16 American standard of living in the 1950s so high that increasing consumption was no longer
E
17 based on satisfying the needs, but on creating artificial wants. On the basis of his empirical
C
18 studies, Easterlin (1974) questioned the assumption that general happiness of a nation would
C
19 increase indefinitely and suggested that saturation would be reached at a certain income level
A
20 (see also Max-Neef 1995). A number of explanations for saturation and/or the negative well-
21 being effects of economic growth were introduced: for example, status consumption as a zero
22 sum game (Hirsch 1977) and consumption as a source of comfort, as opposed to pleasure and
23 joy (Scitovsky 1977).

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
3
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 Publishing the Limits to Growth (Meadows et al. 1972) computer simulations and the
2 simultaneous oil crisis in 1973–74 brought resource scarcity and the ideas of planetary
3 boundaries of economic growth to international attention (Boulding 1968; Georgescu-RToegen
4 1971; Collins 2002). The idea of the steady-state economy was introduced and developed
P
5 further by Daly who envisioned stopping the growth of material production and Iconsumption
R
6 (1996, 1991, and 1974).1 Also, the field of ecological economics was established to take into
C
7 account the material and energy flows between natural and human economies (Røpke 2004).
S
8 In the 1980s, the concept of sustainable development rose to the international agenda after
U
9 the publication of Our Common Future (WCED 1987). In this vastly influential book, sustainable
N
10 development was considered to be realised through economic growth in the developing
A
11 countries, whereas in the developed countries it would be achieved by increased efficiency in
M
12 food and energy production, reallocation of wealth, and sustainable maintenance of natural
13 resources.
D
14 According to Mitcham (1995) sustainable development was from the beginning an
E
15 attempt to reconcile economic growth with the demands for ecological integrity (see also
T
16 Carruthers 2001; Mebratu 1998). Interpreting sustainable development as sustainable growth
P
17 has become mainstream thinking in the official national and international political arenas. At
E
18 the same time growth critique has landed in a marginal position (Carruthers 2001; see also
C
19 Fuchs and Lorek 2005). The signs of marginalisation can be seen, for example, in the Agenda 21
C
20 adopted in 1992 at Rio Earth Summit (UN 1993) and the relatively modest attention given to
A
21 the elaborately updated Limits to Growth book (Meadows et al 1992; 2004). Growth critical
22 aspects are clearly missing in the report of the Rio+20 Conference in 2012 (UNEP 2011). The
23 tendency to strongly emphasise the potential of eco-efficiency while ignoring or even denying
1 See also Kerschner (2010) on the complementarity of degrowth and steady-state.

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
4
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 the possibility of curbing Western consumption prevails in the official environmental agenda.
2 The latest buzzwords, such as ‘green economy’ and ‘green (economic) growth’ (European
3 Commission 2011; OECD 2011; UNEP 2011), follow this line of thought and can be regaTrded as
4 synonyms for ‘sustainable growth.’
P
I
5 Recently, the debate on degrowth has fuelled the renaissance of criticism of
R
6 unchecked economic growth. Degrowth draws from earlier growth critique, especially that of
C
7 Georgescu-Roegen; however, according Demaria et al. (2013), it has various other intellectual
S
8 sources too. Martínez-Alier et al. (2010) describe degrowth as a grassroots movement and an
U
9 academic concept that influence each other. Demaria et al. (2013) also use the term ‘activist-
N
10 led science.’ Schneider et al. (2010) define sustainable degrowth as ‘an equitable down-scaling
A
11 of production and consumption that increases human well-being and enhances ecological
M
12 conditions at the local and global level, in the short and long term.’ They also distinguish
13 sustainable degrowth from unsustainaDble degrowth, that is, recession and depression.
14 According to Fournier (2008), degrowth attempts to repoliticise economics and emphasises
E
15 equality, democracy and citizenship (see also Demaria et al. 2013).
T
P
16 The purpose of this paper is to analyse the themes in the classics of contemporary
E
17 growth critique. The research question is ‘What kind of themes can be defined from the
C
18 central publications?’ The question is divided into four subquestions: 1) What kinds of
C
19 meanings are attached to economic growth? 2) What, precisely, is it in economic growth that
A
20 is being criticised? 3) What kind of forms does the opposition between defenders and critics of
21 growth take? 4) What do the growth critics offer as an alternative to economic growth? The
22 main focus of this article is to answer the first two questions. Questions 3 and 4 are treated
23 only from the perspective of illustrating how different forms of opposition and the various

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
5
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 propositions of growth critics can be positioned within the identified themes. That is to say,
2 questions 3 and 4 are answered in a short and summarising manner and the purpose of this
3 article is not to provide a comprehensive and detailed description of these topics. T
P
4 Section 2 presents the material and methods are introduced. The three core themes
I
5 identified in the material are presented in sections 3, 4 and 5. Finally, the findings are
R
6 summarised and discussed in section 6.
C
7 2 Materials and Methods S
8
U
9 A survey of approximately 30 recent scientific articles related to growth critique in
N
10 general and to degrowth in particular revealed that quite a few of them referred to works of
A
11 three authors – Tim Jackson, Serge Latouche and Peter Victor – and especially to some of their
M
12 latest books. These books were Managing without growth: Slower by design, not disaster
13 (Victor 2009), Farewell to Growth (LatoDuche 2009; French original Petit traité de la
14 décroissance sereine, published 2006), and Prosperity without growth: Economics for a finite
E
15 planet (Jackson 2009). The material of this study comprises these three books, which we
T
16 regard as contemporary classics of growth critique.2 Jackson’s book contains short
P
17 commentaries by Herman Daly, Bill McKibben, Mary Robinson and Pavan Sukhdev; these texts
E
18 were included in the analysis. Since the material represents only growth critique,3 the
C
19 perspectives of the growth advocates are beyond the scope of this paper.
C
A
2 In order to make the text more readable, references to the three books that constitute the research material are
indicated by author name and pagination only (no publication year). For example, (Jackson 39) refers to Jackson’s
Prosperity without Growth, page 39. All other references are indicated with publication year as usual.
3 Latouche has actively participated in the formation of the degrowth concept. Jackson and Victor do not identify
themselves within degrowth in their books. Thus we prefer to use the umbrella term ’growth critique’ instead of the
more specific term ’degrowth’ when referring to the entire research material.

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
6
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 In order to answer the research question, a qualitative content analysis (Elo and
2 Kyngäs 2008; Forman and Damschroder 2008; Graneheim and Lundman 2004;) was conducted
3 on the material. This method can be used to identify the central themes from a text maTss.
4 First, the key meanings and content of the selected meaning units are summarised in a
P
5 compact form. The term ‘meaning unit’ refers to the words, sentences or paragrIaphs of the
R
6 text. Since the material contains of approximately 600 pages of text, the analysis concentrates
C
7 mainly on the paragraph level in order to avoid fragmentation. Selecting the relevant meaning
S
8 units was guided by the research questions. The next step of the analysis was to arrange and
U
9 group the condensed meaning units hierarchically into sub- and supragroups. At the same
N
10 time, the meanings were condensed (and abstracted) further in order to identify the core
A
11 content.
M
12 The qualitative content analysis can be focused on the manifest and/or latent contents
13 of the text. These content types requirDe a varying degree of interpretation, with manifest
14 contents being more obvious and latent contents more ambiguous. Graneheim and Lundman
E
15 (2004) suggest that the terms ‘category’ and ‘theme’ should be used to refer to manifest and
T
16 latent contents, respectively. The terminology used in this study follows this suggestion, as it
P
17 provides transparency with regard to the stage in which interpretation and abstraction begin
E
18 to dominate the analysis. According to Graneheim and Lundman, categories are mutually
C
19 exclusive whereas themes are not, because latent contents are open to multiple
C
20 interpretations.
A
21 The analysis ensures that economic growth is addressed more broadly than simply in
22 terms of GDP growth. Essentially, growth critique is a critique of growth societies, covering not
23 only economic activity but also a wide range of social phenomena and political processes.

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
7
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 There are several ways to distinguish between different aspects of growth. In the research
2 material, Latouche proposes a distinction between growth ‘as [an] evolutionary phenomen[on]
3 affecting specific realities (population, potato production, quantities of waste, toxicity oTf
4 water, etc.)’ and ‘as [an] abstract concept referring to an economic dynamism that is an end in
P
5 itself.’ Spangenberg (2010) differentiates between growth and growth policy, sinIce they have
R
6 different effects. Kerschner (2010) distinguishes three aspects of growth: growth discourse as
C
7 a driving force, growth policy as a pressure, and the real impacts of economic growth. In
S
8 contrast to these proposals, the suggestion put forward in this paper is based on a qualitative
U
9 content analysis of degrowth literature. As a result of the analysis, three central themes in the
N
10 21st century growth critique were identified from the material: growth as a phenomenon,
A
11 growth as an institution and growth as an ideology. Each theme offers a different point of view
M
12 to economic growth and to the research questions. In the following sections, these themes are
13 presented separately.
D
14 3 Growth as Phenomenon
E
15
T
16 ‘The myth of growth has failed us. It has failed the 1 billion people who still attempt
P
17 to live on half the price of a cup of coffee each day. It has failed the fragile ecological
E
18 systems on which we depend for survival.’ (Jackson 15)
C
19 The first theme examined is ‘growth as a phenomenon’ which deals with the concrete
C
20 consequences of economic growth. From this point of view, the critique is targeted towards
A
21 the growing negative effects and decreasing positive effects of economic growth. Jackson and,
22 especially, Victor put a lot of effort into building their case by using a set of indicators. In
23 Latouche’s book, the problematic nature of economic growth is the starting point rather than
24 the conclusion.

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
8
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 The consequences of economic growth discussed in the books fall into two categories:
2 environmental effects and well-being effects. When examining the environmental effects of
3 economic growth, the authors concentrate on the negative effects. The possibility of poTsitive
4 effects – as described in the environmental Kuznets curve hypothesis (see e.g. Ang and Liu
P
5 2006; Ayres 2008; Munasinghe 1996;) – is only briefly touched upon by Jackson (I76) and Victor
R
6 (164–5). They argue that the hypothesis holds true only for the local and easily-remedied
C
7 problems. What is more, Victor considers that technical solutions to local problems sometimes
S
8 contribute to global ecological crisis.
U
9 Latouche (e.g. 23–5, 33) discusses environmental problems on a general level using
N
10 the comprehensive term ‘environmental crisis’ and referring mostly to the ecological footprint.
A
11 Jackson (6–14, 32–33, 67–86) and Victor (47–123), on the other hand, are more specific and
M
12 consider environmental problems from the viewpoint of resource scarcity, sinks and life-
13 supporting ecosystem services. AccorDding to Jackson and Victor, these three together impose
14 biophysical limits on growth. Violation of these limits is seen as a threat to long-term
E
15 sustainability and to the possibility of future generations to flourish (Latouche 23–5, 31;
T
16 Jackson 32–33, 45; Victor 43–44, 47).
P
E
17 When referring to past and currently occurring environmental problems, the authors
C
18 most often simply state that economic growth is their main cause (e.g. Daly in Jackson 267;
C
19 Jackson 13, 121; Victor 98). However, when considering the future, the argumentation
A
20 becomes more refined and elaborate. Jackson (77–82) and Victor (102–23) utilise the IPAT
21 equation (see York et al. 2003 and Waggoner and Ausubel 2002 for IPAT in general). Victor
22 (99–123) also discerns the scale, composition and technology of the economy. Thus, it

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
9
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 becomes clear that the volume of the economy is not the only factor behind ecological
2 distress.
T
3 The key question here is whether environmental problems can significantly be
P
4 ameliorated by technological means while sustaining economic growth. In other words, is
I
5 absolute decoupling possible? Jackson (67–86) and Victor (54–59, 70, 173–6) make a
R
6 distinction between absolute and relative decoupling (a more refined distinction is provided by
C
7 Tapio 2005). In absolute decoupling, environmental impacts decline even if the economy
S
8 grows. Relative decoupling indicates a situation where the environmental impacts still grow,
U
9 but the economy grows faster. Since the environmental impacts are already on an
N
10 unsustainable level, absolute decline is needed. Jackson and Victor raise two questions in
A
11 regard to absolute decoupling.
M
12 Firstly, is absolute decoupling already occurring? Jackson (67–86) and Victor (54–59,
D
13 70, 107–123) deny this (see also Bithas and Kalimeris 2013 on the global aggregate level of
E
14 decoupling). Jackson mentions certain Western countries where the growth of environmental
T
15 impacts has levelled off despite rising GDP. He points out that this improvement is more
P
16 apparent than real, however, because these countries have externalised production and
E
17 environmental problems to the Third World (Jackson 73–75, 129; see also empirical evidence
C
18 in Mattila 2011 and Peters et al. 2011).
C
19 Secondly, is absolute decoupling probable in future? Again, the answers provided by
A
20 Jackson (14, 68–86, 121–2, 187–8) and Victor (107–123, 173–6) are negative since the actual
21 improvement rates in eco-efficiency comprise only a fraction of the required rates. They
22 conclude that absolute decoupling is a myth, an unattainable technological dream. Thus, they
23 reject the highly popular vision of green growth, arguing that there is an inescapable

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
10
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 contradiction between continuous growth and environmental protection (see also Latouche
2 11, 55–6). According to Jackson (95) and Victor (110–1), the rebound effect will undermine the
3 potential of technological solutions even further.4 They conclude that, alongside technoTlogical
4 improvements, the scale of the economy has to be addressed as well.5
P
I
5 The social effects of economic growth are also discussed in the books. While
R
6 recognising the suffering caused by the inability to meet one’s basic needs, Latouche is
C
7 sceptical about the benefits of economic growth and the whole concept of progress (16–20,
S
8 52–65). Jackson and Victor, for their part, examine the subject in a more detailed and broad
U
9 manner than Latouche. They use statistical data and compare GDP to more specific welfare
N
10 indicators. Jackson and Victor do not deny the past achievements of economic growth in
A
11 improving health, prolonging human life, etc., but they also remind that the problems of
M
12 poverty and inequality as well as unemployment persist in spite of economic growth. Jackson
13 (55–62) also points out that, statisticalDly, some middle and low income countries rank
14 remarkably high in one or more basic components of well-being, thus suggesting that the
E
15 causal relationship between income and well-being is not clear and constant. What is more,
T
16 Jackson (5, 40–42, 50–65) and Victor (124–68, 129–133) conclude that economic growth has
P
17 long since ceased to increase well-being and happiness of Western people. Jackson (40–41)
E
C
4 On different definitions and estimates of the rebound effect see e.g. Berkhout et al. (2000), Binswanger (2011) and
Greening et al. (2000). Alfredsson (2004) has conducted an interesting empirical study on green consumption and its
C
rebound effect in Swedish households. Alcott (2010 and 2008) and Figge et al. (2014) discuss the occurrence of
rebound effects in the context of sufficiency, and Schneider (2008) analyses the concept in the context of degrowth.
5 In contrast, A none of the authors suggest controlling population growth as a means to relieve environmental
pressures. The books refer to the morally problematic nature of influencing fertility rates and take the estimated
population growth as a given. Jackson (77), however, implies that also high fertility rates can be morally problematic if
they are not based on freedom of choice. Latouche (25–29) regards the reduction of population as ’a false solution.’
He argues that the humanity should first tackle the problems of excess consumption and inequitable distribution of
resources, and only after that can the population issue be addressed calmly and rationally. In contrast, Victor (24, 194)
states that a socially sustainable non-growing economy would also require a non-growing population (see also
Kerschner 2010). Nevertheless, Victor does not propose any measures for controlling fertility rates. This is due to the
fact that he treats mostly the case of Canada, in which fertility rates are already low and the population is ageing.
Thus, Victor suggests only minor alterations to the Canadian policy of work-related immigration.

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
11
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 and Victor (126) both refer to a level of approximately $15,000 GDP per capita after which
2 increases in GDP hardly contribute to well-being (see also Max-Neef 1995). As Victor ironically
3 states, North Americans and the West in general ‘have been more successful in decoupTling
4 GDP from happiness than in decoupling it from material and energy’ (125).
P
I
5 Explanations for this divergence between well-being or happiness and economic
R
6 growth are manifold, and the following summary does not do justice to the richness of detail in
C
7 the research material. Victor and Jackson delve into this subject more explicitly and
S
8 systematically. Firstly, Jackson (40–41, 55–61) appeals to the diminishing marginal utility of
U
9 rising incomes and economic growth, that is, the fact that the benefits of incremental growth
N
10 decrease while the costs increase (see also Daly in Jackson 268). In addition, all three authors
A
11 refer to negative well-being effects of growth, such as stress, unrewarding work, and
M
12 weakening communities and social relations (Jackson 101, 144, 147–8; Latouche 16–20, 54,
13 81–88; Victor 154). Secondly, Jackson D(39–40, 125–6, 179–80) and Victor (9–10, 129–31)
14 mention the well-known criticisms of GDP as a measure of well-being, such as the inclusion of
E
15 aspects that decrease well-being; the exclusion of factors that increase well-being; and lack of
T
16 attention paid to income distribution; (see also van den Bergh 2010 and 2009; Giannetti 2015).
P
17 Thirdly, the books discuss to the idea of people getting used to a higher standard of living and
E
18 adjusting their aspirations accordingly (Jackson 41; Victor 127). This type of adaptation also
C
19 explains why a reduction in the current levels of Western consumption would result in a
C
20 (temporary) feeling of deprivation even if basic needs were still met (see e.g. Matthey 2010).
A
21 The fourth argument is, in brief, that happiness and contentment are partly affected by the
22 relative status and position, especially after the basic needs are met. A rise in the overall
23 standard of living does not affect relative positions; however, the questions of income

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
12
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 distribution and inequality remain significant. (Jackson 50–55, 146–8; Latouche 37; Victor 131–
2 51.)
T
3 Nevertheless, Victor (18, 24–5, 98) and Jackson (40–41) believe that non-Western
P
4 countries would still benefit from economic growth. In fact, one of Victor’s (vi, 98, 111–2, 223)
I
5 main proposals is that, in a world with limits to growth, the Western countries should abandon
R
6 growth in order to make room for other regions’ economies to grow. They argue that, in these
C
7 countries, the standard of living is still comparatively low, which means that the marginal
S
8 utility is higher and the threshold after which rising incomes cease to contribute to well-being
U
9 has not been reached yet. Victor, however, is doubtful of emphasising growth over equality. In
N
10 other words, he implicitly raises the question of how the benefits of non-Western growth
A
11 would and should be shared. Latouche (56–65), instead, warns against the perils of growth-
M
12 dependency and Westernization, encouraging the people of the Third World to create and
13 strive for their own visions of success aDnd well-being.
E
14 From the perspective of growth as phenomenon, the overall conclusion of the books is
T
15 that, in the Western countries, the negative effects of economic growth override the positive
P
16 ones. This is aptly summarised by Herman Daly in the commentary of Jackson’s book (268): we
E
17 ‘have entered an era of uneconomic growth.’
C
18 Under the phenomenon theme, the controversy between the critics and the defenders
C
19 of economic growth revolves around the true and correct interpretations of empirical data on
A
20 well-being, environmental effects, and eco-efficiency brought about by technological
21 advancements, with both sides of the controversy contesting for the most convincing
22 arguments (see also Daly 1997; Solow 1997; Stiglitz 1997). The information and data about the
23 effects of economic growth is plentiful, fragmented, and open to multiple interpretations.

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
13
Economic growth as phenomenon, institution and ideology:
A qualitative content analysis of the 21st century growth critique
1 Thus, the critics rather successfully convince the reader that those believing in sustainable
2 growth might be wrong. The question is, however, can they convince the reader that they
3 themselves are right? T
P
4 According to the authors, concentrating on economic growth results in losing focus on
I
5 the things that really matter. Instead of striving for overall economic growth, all three books
R
6 make a case for more precisely defined social and ecological goals (Jackson 122, 194; Latouche
C
7 13; Victor 2, 184). They argue that if these goals are achieved, it should not matter whether
S
8 the economy grows or diminishes. Thus, the authors promote a nonchalant attitude towards
U
9 the size of the economy, that is, ‘agrowth’ (e.g. Jackson 141, 197; Latouche 8; Victor 1, 184.)
N
10 Recently, there has been a debate on whether one should resist the centrality of economic
A
11 growth explicitly or adopt the agrowth approach (see Kallis 2011; van den Bergh 2011; van den
M
12 Bergh and Kallis 2012).
D
13 In addition, none of the three authors condemn all growth. They support the idea of
E

R. G. A. Williams
Logical analysis as a qualitative method I:
Themes in old age and chronic illness
Abstract Qualitative methods have been criticized for their lack of explicit
procedures and weakness in explanation. The present paper draws
attention to a qualitative approach with a clear procedure and wide
explanatory scope - logical analysis. Logic has been neglected as a way
of organizing informants' accounts because it has been identified
with a procedure for organizing theory. In this paper, the attempt is to
reverse the emphasis, and to demonstrate a way of working with
informants rather than involving in theoretical prescriptions. The
approach is illustrated by some themes arising in old age and chronic
illness.
First, two conceptions of illness which have been distinguished in
the work of Claudine Herzlich are analysed as systems of premises and
consequences. Next, the procedures involved in logical analysis, and the
explanations and practical uses which arise from it, are illustrated in
two case studies. These cases are part of a larger body of data collected,
amongst other things, for the purpose of eliciting the logic of old
people's thinking.
The emphasis is on illustrating the method; and general issues which
arise from it, including the analysis of people who entertain contra-
dictory systems of thought, are postponed to a second paper.
Introduction
Qualitative methods have held an enduring place in sociology despite
considerable and often well-founded criticism. Some of that criticism
has been directed to identifying the appropriate topics for such methods,
and to restricting their invasion of inappropriate areas. Other comments
have pointed out the vagueness of qualitative studies about their pro-
cedures of data collection and analysis, and their weakness in providing
general explanations; and a growing literature has discussed ways of
repairing these faults.' A method which seems to avoid many notorious
faults, and to illuminate a specific topic, is offered in this paper.
Among the appropriate topics for qualitative methods it is normal
to include questions about reasons as opposed to situational causes.

Logical analysis as a qualitative method: I 141
about values as opposed to institutions, or about cultural meanings as
opposed to structural constraints. The relation between internal meanings
and extemal situations, for instance, has become the focus of the popular
'career' study which traces the experience of individuals over time as they
come into contact with a major public institution. Less popular than the
subject of 'careers' though, and in many ways unrecognized because it
may be seen merely as a marginal aspect of a 'career' study, is the equally
important topic of how internal meanings are related to one another.
This topic, the interconnection of meanings, is that for which a quali-
tative method is suggested here. The method proposed is an adaptation
of something long established in another discipline — formal logical
analysis. Logic has the great advantage in this respect that its procedures
of analysis are clear, and its canons of explanation are perhaps the
oldest in the business. Certain humble uses of these virtues, though,
have been obscured by the sophisticated functions of symbolic logic in
philosophy and the natural sciences. In philosophy, symbolic logic has
been used to exhibit the nature of logical form when denuded of
content. In the natural sciences, symbolic languages have been used to
build theoretical assumptions and to derive new consequences from
them. Resistance to these models of analytic procedure has consumed
much ink in sociology, with good reason; and these are not the uses
proposed here. The proposition here is for logic to be used without its
symbolic paraphemalia simply to reveal the logical shape of an inform-
ant's ideas. Instead of measuring the informant against the researcher's
logic, the research attempts to elicit the informant's logic. But the
procedure is more easily demonstrated than discussed, and the emphasis
of this paper is solely on demonstration.
The method will be worked through on the topic of old age and
chronic illness, leaving to a later paper the theoretical issues which arise.
Ageing and disablement have been studied extensively in recent years,
but the literature mainly deals with the extemal circumstances of the
old people concemed. 'Career' studies, in which the intemal experience
of those circumstances might have been illuminated, have on the whole
been lacking; and while work has now begun to emerge on the world of
older people as they currently perceive it,^ some sociologists have
rightly wished to see in addition a proper value given to the influence of
biography on that world.^ To some, though, biographical study on the
themes of old age, for all its evident attraction, has seemed a hopeless
ideal, and it would indeed be hopeless if one sought to establish causal
relations between present circumstances and events as they were long
ago, rather than as an old person now thinks that they were. But what
people think of past events - the set of conclusions which they draw
from remembered experiences — is itself of great importance, and

likely to be appropriate.
Definitions of illness and disability also vary, though, under the
influence of a whole constellation of current cultural conceptions; and
an excellent example of such cultural vadations is the study by Claudine
Herzlich on middle-class Padsians.* I have capitalized on her work by
subjecting to logical analysis some of the conceptions of illness which
she has distinguished, and this will give a preliminary example of what
is entailed in the approach. It is not merely as an illustration, though,
that her work is important; I hope also to show that it gives dse to a
general explanatory scheme of considerable power.
In order to reveal the logical form of Herzlich's matedal, I shall
render the attitudes descdbed by her as a sequence of propositions. In
doing so, it is impossible to 'shdnk' the number of words used by the
author without losing meaning, but this is permissible, as a generalization
is permissible, in order to handle wider connections. The point is there-
fore not faithfulness to the text at all costs, but the extraction of
essential sequences of thought which may subsequently be compared
with other matedal. However, as realism is important in proceeding
from connection to connection, I will disregard some conventions,
particularly in the text, in the way I state propositions and logical
sequences. In the figures, though, and in the conclusions on each case
study, I will make a more formal presentation of premises, although only
to a degree sufficient for sociological purposes.'
An illustration of logical analysis from the literature — Herzlich's study
The study by Claudine Herzlich on health and illness is in fact quite an
old one, although its publication in English has been more recent, and
its lack of influence in Bdtish and Amedcan medical sociology to date
is undoubtedly due in part to its unfamiliar approach. It is also due,
though, to the rather high level of generality at which its conclusions
appear to operate, and the lack of any context in the way of illness
behaviour or family negotiation which might lend realism to what
are essentially the contents of a speculative conversation between the
interviewer and the respondent. However, credibility is lent to her con-
clusions by their correspondence with, and addition of detail to, themes
which occur in more orthodox medical sociology. The concept of
'normalizing' for instance, has close resemblances to Herzlich's concept
of illness as an occupation', and the concept of 'disassociation'
appears to be mirrored in her 'illness as a destroyer'.* Herzlich also,

Herzlich's category of 'illness as a destroyer' then, begins with
premises something Hke these:
If I am active, then I am not ill.
If I am myself, then I am active.
I have something to offer if, and only if, I am active.
The consequences of these three premises, which are so innocuous at
first sight, are surprisingly extensive, and soon begin to imply definitions
of the sick, behaviour towards the sick, and behaviour as a sick person.
Notably, though, at this stage only one of the premises actually mentions
illness. Here are some initial consequences of recognizing 'I am ill':
I am not myself (or as it is sometimes expressed, 'I' am 'dead').
1 do not have something to offer.
then

therefore
I cannot repay help,
but usually

so

Parallel consequences will of course follow from the recognition
'You are ill', and result in avoidance of the sick, or a patronizing or
pitying treatment of their needs. The terrible altematives which this
line of connection throws up may then lead anybody who holds these
premises to answer the question 'Am I ill?' or 'Are you ill?' with a re-
affirmation of the first premise as asolution to the question, one which,
however, in this context and use, acquires a new connotation:
If I am active, then I am not ill.
Then other commonplace premises are at once brought into play:

I act ill if, and only if, I am ill.
From which it follows that
I do not need a medical diagnosis.
I am not seen taking medicine.
But once it is no longer possible to deny 'I am ill' in the face of the
definitions of all about one, some other premises may be brought into
play with further interesting consequences.
If 'I' am 'dead', then I have nothing to fear from death.
If I have nothing to fear from death, then the doctor can do what he Ukes.
These two polar reactions, involving refusal of medical information,
surreptitious preventive efforts, irritation with help and fierce denials
on the one hand, and helpless compliance, childishness, and careless-
ness of the outcome on the other, present I suspect, an all-too-recogniz-
able portrait of one kind of patient — a 'bad' patient when there is
disease and the doctor is diagnosing it, or when the disease is chronic,
but a 'good' patient when there is no serious disease, since he will not
complain of ambiguous symptoms, and in some respects a 'good'
patient on whom to operate. Thus 'bad' or 'good' is merely contingent,
and this patient's behaviour emerges throughout as the remorselessly
rational consequence of sensible propositions. The whole system of
thought is summarized formally in Figure 1.
'Illness as an occupation' is in some respects the antithesis of 'illness
as a destroyer', but as a system of thought it derives from premises
which are not merely antithetical. Indeed a number of important
premises which have nothing specific to do with illness, can be shared
by both systems. These are:
If I am myself, then I am active.
I have something to offer if, and only if, I am active.
If one does not have something to offer, then one cannot repay help.
Either one repays help, or else one is a child.
In some ways the other premises of this way of thinking may also look
suspiciously like those which made the definition of illness as 'a des-
troyer'. Two of them might run something like this:
If I am healthy, then I am strong.
If I am strong, then I am active.
But - and this is the key to this mode of seeing the world — it does not
follow from these premises that
If I am active, then I am not ill.

The consequences of this one vital shift of premise are immediate,
for because of this shift it remains possible to say that:
1 have something to offer.
I am myself.
1 can repay help.
1 am not a child.
and relations are free to continue to develop between myself as a

The new premise also influences the definition of doctors, and
the value of the sick person's own activities. The central idea of 'fight-
ing' has a number of corollaries:
If 1 fight, then 1 fight well.
If 1 fight well, then 1 cut losses and develop any resources 1 can find.
Now although there is nothing in the present way of thinking to prevent
people from asking questions about their illness and taking medicines
openly, there is also something which naturally impels them in this
direction. It can be stated like this:
If 1 do not demand explanations, 1 do not find out what 1 am fighting.
If I do not find out what I'm fighting, 1 do not fight well.
Hence it is charactedstic of this system of thought that the doctor is
cross-questioned and his orders constantly appraised for cladty and
consistency. Naturally, a patient who thinks like this can be very dif-
ficult, although he is a model patient from the point of view of having
'spirit'. He also not only saves what he can from the wreck, but searches
for new resources, whether activities or social connections, which can
help to sustain him. In this sense.
If I fight well, then 1 am strong.
And strength is seen to come not only from health, but from the pro-
cess of the struggle itself. Again, the whole conception of health and ill-
ness in this way of thinking can be represented formally, as in Figure 2.
Two partly contrasting conceptions of illness have now been analysed.
But the analysis, at this stage, may still bear a resemblance to the logical
construction of theory in the abstract, because no reference has been
made to the thinking of specific informants. Nevertheless the prop-
ositions differ from theoretical propositions in having, for the most
part, a first person subject, for all that the subject is not identified.

Two case studies in systems of thought about illness
The Scottish data which I will now draw on have been collected,
amongst other considerations, for the purpose of eliciting the logic of
informants' ideas. As regards the choice of informants, people over
sixty years of age were approached in a working-class and a middle-
class area through the medium of social clubs. From these initial
contacts, introductions were obtained, carefully varied by age, sex,
and marital status, and most particularly by whether they belonged
to clubs or not, with the aim of maintaining proportions in each
category similar to those found in national data. The interviewing of
these people has all been done by the author, and there have been a
number of repeated interviews, and some informal social contact as
well. Everybody was asked to talk informally about how health had
affected, and was affecting, their lives. The early questioning elicited
health history and residential history, but thereafter it proceeded on
positions already taken, seeking to clarify them particularly in relation
to future expectations of illness and dying, and planning decisions
related thereto. Afterwards, fresh thinking and behaviour related to
health and illness were picked up in later interviews. Also, as a further
check on the interpretation, the design has facilitated cross-references
by some informants to the behaviour of others. The study is still
developing, but at the time of writing the pool of data included tape
transcripts or field notes on conversations with 41 working-class people
in 30 households, and 28 middle-class people in 22 households.
From this material I have selected two case studies to develop the
content of Herzlich's insight in relation to logical analysis. The first is
a widow in her late seventies from the working-class area whose thought
approximates closely to the type christened by Herzlich, 'Illness as a
destroyer'. The second is a widow in her late sixties from the middle-
class area whose way of thinking approximates to the other type,
'Illness as an occupation'. Both cases are chosen because they present
these systems of thought in a form which is virtually complete and
unqualified. Both are people who strike one as very much 'all of a
piece'. They may puzzle over decisions and conclude afterwards that
they made mistakes, hut they continue to identify both their correct
decisions and their mistakes in the same coherent terms. In this, of
course, they differ from the sort of person who, like most of us, is
going to present the obvious problem, as well as the most interesting
opportunity, for the analysis of premises: the person who entertains
contradictions. This case will, however, be dealt with in another paper.
The present two case studies will develop the portrait of the two
systems of thought about illness, and will reveal most of the initial

My treatment of the two cases varies progressively. In the first
study I pay special attention to the process of leaming the logic of
the informant's idioms and translating them into the terms of each
system of thought. Herzlich's informants were middle class, because
she felt that this class had an active role in 'the genesis, transformation
and renewal of ideologies'.'' Since this suggestion implies that her
analysis might work best for the highly articulate, I have chosen for
this study what ought to be the difficult case — the working-class
widow, Mrs Stone. Also, in the conclusions on Mrs Stone, I spend time
on discussing the formal requirements of this type of explanation. The
formal requirements of the explanation and the process of translation are
then largely taken for granted in the second study of Mrs Hannay, making
her study the shorter, although the volume of material collected on Mrs
Hannay was actually the more extensive. In the conclusions on each
study, I also draw out possible practical uses of the method.

Conclusions on Mrs Stone
1 have sought to show how one proceeds with a logical analysis of Mrs
Stone's thoughts and behaviour in her own terms. After analysis, the
next step is explanation. In a formal explanation of this kind, taking
any one consequence in Mrs Stone's behaviour or thought, an economical
set of her premises can be stated which explain the consequence, given
three main conditions:
(a) that the investigator has learnt Mrs Stone's language and logic
correctly;
(b) that there is no reason to invalidate any of Mrs Stone's premises
as rationalizations, on the grounds that they cost her nothing and do
no work other than justifying one specific response;
(c) that no premise antecedent to the premises stated countermands
their application to emerging consequences.
Subject to these three conditions, Mrs Stone's explanation of her'
statements and behaviour has a. prima facie vahdity, though it makes no
claims to be complete. Its connections with other premises, and similarly
with situations which give rise to the premises held, can be elaborated
indefinitely. But thus far it has a fair claim to be valid.
Next, in order to see Mrs Stone's explanation as an instance of a
general system of thought, it is necessary to translate, making equi-
valences between the propositions and terms of her system and the
general system. This process takes place subject to a fourth condition:
(d) the investigator's translations are acceptable.
All these conditions for the validity of the explanation can now be
reviewed. It is convenient to take condition (a), the investigator's learning
of the informant's logic, and condition (d), his translations into the
general system, together, since both are essentially tested by inspection.
